q: What is gross income?
r: The total amount earned before taxes and deductions
It is the starting point for figuring take-home pay.
w: The amount left after paying taxes and deductions
The amount saved each month for emergencies
The amount spent on needs each month

q: What is net income (take-home pay)?
r: The amount left after taxes and deductions are taken out
It is the money available to spend or save.
w: The total amount earned before any deductions
The amount an employer pays in payroll taxes
The amount of a yearly bonus

q: Maya earns $20 an hour and works 30 hours in a week. What is her gross pay for the week?
r: $20 x 30 hours equals $600.

q: A worker earns $16 an hour. Overtime is paid at 1.5 times the hourly rate for hours over 40. What is the overtime rate?
r: $24 per hour
$16 x 1.5 equals $24.

q: What is a W-4 form used for?
r: Telling an employer how much income tax to withhold
It reflects filing status and adjustments.
w: Reporting total yearly wages to the IRS
That is done on the tax return.

q: What is a W-2 form?
r: A form showing yearly wages and taxes withheld by an employer
Employees use it to file taxes.
w: A form that sets the amount of income tax withheld
A form that reports income for contractors
A form for applying for a job

q: Which deduction is withheld from most paychecks to fund Social Security and Medicare?
r: FICA tax
It is a payroll tax paid by employees and employers.

q: What is a tip?
r: Money a customer gives for service on top of the price
Tips are taxable income.

q: What is the main difference between an employee and an independent contractor?
r: Employers withhold taxes for employees, but contractors pay their own taxes
Contractors control how they work.
w: Employees choose their own hours always

q: Which is an example of passive income?
r: Rent received from a property you own
It comes with little ongoing effort.

q: Which is an example of earned income?
r: Wages from a part-time job
Earned income comes from working.

q: What is a bonus?
r: Extra pay on top of regular wages for good performance or results
It may be one-time or yearly.
w: A fixed amount deducted for insurance
A loan advanced by the employer

q: What is a commission?
r: Pay based on a percentage of sales a worker makes
It rewards sales performance.
w: Pay based on a fixed yearly amount

q: A salesperson earns a 4% commission on $25,000 of sales. What is the commission?
Which employee benefit usually has the greatest financial value?
r: Employer-paid health insurance
It can save thousands of dollars each year.

q: What does an employer 401(k) match mean?
r: The employer adds money based on the employee's own contributions
It increases retirement savings.
w: The employer takes money from the employee's account
The employer lends the employee money
The employer charges a fee for joining

q: What is a minimum wage?
r: The lowest hourly pay an employer may legally pay a covered worker
It is set by law.
w: It is a minimum, not a maximum.

q: Why does education generally increase earning potential?
r: Workers with more education tend to have skills that employers pay more for
Skills and credentials raise value.
w: Education reduces the need to work
Education guarantees a job without effort

q: What is a side hustle?
r: Extra work done to earn additional income outside a main job
It can help reach financial goals.
w: A tax form for extra jobs

q: A teen earns $400 from mowing lawns on their own. Who is responsible for reporting that income?
r: The teen, who may need to report self-employment income
Self-employed earnings can be taxable.
w: No one, because lawn mowing is exempt
Customers usually do not report it.

q: What is a pay stub?
r: A record of gross pay, deductions and net pay for a pay period
It shows how pay is calculated.
w: A bill sent to the employee
It is not a tax return.

q: A pay stub shows gross pay of $800, taxes of $120 and insurance of $30. What is net pay?
What is the difference between a need and a want?
r: A need is essential to live; a want is something you would like to have
Food and shelter are needs.
w: A need costs less than a want
Cost does not decide the difference.
A want is required by law
A need is something you save for

q: Which is the best first step before making a large purchase?
r: Compare prices and features from several sellers
Comparison helps find the best value.
w: Buy from the first store you visit
Ask a friend to buy it for you

q: What is comparison shopping?
r: Checking prices and quality at different stores before buying
It helps get the best value.
w: Buying the most expensive version of a product

q: What is unit pricing?
r: The cost per unit of measure, such as per ounce
It helps compare package sizes.
w: The total cost of a shopping trip

q: A 16 oz bottle costs $3.20 and a 24 oz bottle costs $4.20. Which is the better unit price?
r: The 24 oz bottle at $0.175 per ounce
$4.20 divided by 24 is lower than $3.20 divided by 16.
w: The 16 oz bottle at $0.20 per ounce

q: What is impulse buying?
r: Making an unplanned purchase on a sudden urge
It can break a budget.
w: Buying only what is on a planned list

q: Which habit best prevents impulse buying?
r: Waiting a day before buying non-essential items
Time lets the urge pass.
w: Saving credit card numbers in every app

q: What is a budget?
r: A plan for how to use income for spending, saving and giving
It matches money to priorities.
w: A record of spending after it happens only
A list of items on sale

q: Which expense is variable?
r: Money spent on entertainment each month
It can change each month.

q: Which expense is fixed?
r: Monthly rent
It is the same amount each month.

q: After tracking spending, a student finds $120 a month goes to snacks and only $40 to savings. What is the best adjustment?
r: Reduce snack spending and move the difference toward savings
Aligning spending with goals improves savings.
w: Increase snack spending to balance the budget
Stop tracking spending to avoid stress

q: What is an opportunity cost of spending $50 on a game?
r: What else that $50 could have been used for
Each dollar can be used only once.

q: What is a warranty?
r: A promise from a seller to repair or replace a defective product
Terms and length vary.

q: What should you check before agreeing to a free trial that asks for a card?
r: Whether it renews into a paid subscription and how to cancel
Auto-renewals can cause surprise charges.
w: Nothing, because free trials are always free

q: What is a return policy?
r: A store's rules for returning or exchanging purchases
Policies vary by store.
w: A law that forces refunds on all purchases
It is not an advertising rule.

q: Which action best protects you from online shopping scams?
r: Buying from secure, reputable sites and checking reviews
Trusted sites lower risk.
w: Sending money by gift cards to a seller
Gift cards are hard to recover.
Sharing your password to speed up checkout

q: What is a sales tax?
r: A tax added to the price of goods and services at purchase
Sellers collect it for the government.

q: A jacket costs $60 and the sales tax rate is 8%. What is the total price?
r: $60 plus $4.80 of tax equals $64.80.

q: Why is saving money important?
r: It prepares you for emergencies and future goals
Savings provide security.
w: It removes the need for a budget
It guarantees you will never need a job

q: What is an emergency fund?
r: Money set aside for unexpected expenses such as car repairs or job loss
A common goal is three to six months of expenses.
w: Money set aside for a planned vacation
Money invested in stocks for growth

q: Where should an emergency fund generally be kept?
r: In a safe, easily accessible account such as a savings account
Emergency money must be available quickly.
w: In a long-term account with penalties
It is unsafe and earns nothing.

q: What is interest on a savings account?
r: Money the bank pays you for keeping your money there
It is usually a percentage.
w: A fee you pay for withdrawing

q: What is compound interest?
r: Interest earned on both the original deposit and previous interest
Balances grow faster over time.
w: Interest earned only on the original deposit

q: Which account will grow the most over 10 years, if all have the same rate?
r: The one that compounds most often
More frequent compounding adds interest sooner.
w: The one that pays simple interest
The one with the highest fees only

q: What is the main advantage of starting to save early?
r: Compound interest has more time to grow your money
Time multiplies growth.
w: You can spend all your income
Saving early does not allow that.
You will never need to save again
Rates do not depend on age.

q: What is a certificate of deposit (CD)?
r: A savings product that holds money for a set term at a fixed rate
Early withdrawal may bring a penalty.
w: A checking account with unlimited withdrawals
A CD is not a stock.

q: What does FDIC insurance protect?
r: Bank deposits up to the legal limit if a bank fails
The standard limit is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
w: Stocks you own through a broker
The FDIC does not insure investments.

q: A person has $300,000 in one account at a single FDIC-insured bank. How much is insured, in the standard individual case?
r: That is the standard limit.
w: Deposits are insured up to the limit.

q: What is a savings goal?
r: A specific amount of money you plan to save by a certain time
Goals give saving a purpose.
w: A fee charged by a bank
It is not a loan plan.

q: Leo wants $600 in 6 months. How much must he save each month?
r: $600 divided by 6 equals $100.

q: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
r: Moving money to savings before spending on other things
Saving becomes a priority.

q: What is automatic saving?
r: Setting up regular transfers into savings without needing to remember
Consistency builds the habit.

q: What is the Rule of 72 used for?
r: Estimating how long it takes money to double at a given interest rate
Divide 72 by the rate.
w: It is not for retirement age.

q: Using the Rule of 72, about how many years will it take money earning 4% to double?
r: 18 years
72 divided by 4 equals 18.

q: What is a high-yield savings account?
r: A savings account that pays a higher interest rate than a typical one
Online banks often offer them.
w: A checking account with no interest
It is not a stock account.

q: What is inflation's effect on savings kept in cash?
r: Purchasing power declines over time
Prices rise while the cash stays the same.

q: A savings account pays 1% interest while inflation is 3%. What is happening to the real value of the savings?
r: It is decreasing because inflation outpaces interest
Real return is negative.
w: It is increasing because interest is positive
It is staying exactly the same

q: What is the main purpose of a college savings plan such as a 529?
r: To save for education expenses with tax advantages
Qualified withdrawals can be tax-free.

q: Which of these is a good reason to keep money in a savings account instead of a checking account?
r: Savings accounts usually pay interest
Checking often pays little or none.
w: Savings accounts allow unlimited check writing

q: What is the main reason to read a contract before signing?
r: To understand your rights, fees and obligations
Surprises can be costly.
w: To make the document last longer
To avoid talking to the seller
To make sure the font is readable

q: A buyer is told 'sign now or lose the deal' on a big purchase. What is the smartest reaction?
r: Slow down, compare options and read the terms
Pressure tactics are a warning sign.
w: Sign immediately to avoid missing out
Sign without reading to save time
Share financial details with the seller

q: Which payment method gives the strongest protection against unauthorized charges in many cases?
r: A credit card
Federal law limits cardholder liability and allows disputes.
w: Lost cash is hard to recover.
Lost gift cards are hard to recover.
Wire transfers are hard to reverse.

q: What is a consumer right?
r: The right to be informed and to be protected from unsafe or deceptive products
Agencies enforce these protections.
w: The right to buy anything for free
The right to ignore store policies
The right to avoid sales tax

q: Which agency helps protect consumers from deceptive advertising?
r: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
It enforces truth-in-advertising rules.
